Trying to Conceive

Fertility supplements: evidence, ingredients and safer choices

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A fertility supplement may contain vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids or hormones. These ingredients do different things, and a product marketed for egg quality, sperm health or conception is not necessarily proven to increase the chance of having a baby. Separate nutritional care from optional fertility add-ons before choosing a bottle.

Start with the purpose, not the promise

Correcting a deficiency and preparing for pregnancy are worthwhile goals. They differ from treating infertility. A prenatal supplement supports nutritional needs; a fertility blend may add substances whose benefits and pregnancy safety are uncertain. Neither replaces a varied diet or assessment of a fertility problem.

If you could become pregnant, folic acid is recommended even without a diagnosed deficiency. A usual recommendation is 400 micrograms daily before conception and through the first 12 weeks; some people need a prescribed higher dose. Follow local guidance and your clinician’s plan. This prevents neural tube defects; it is not a guaranteed way to conceive.

What counts as convincing evidence?

A nutrient’s role in cells, an animal experiment or a blood-level association does not show that taking more improves fertility. Ovulation, sperm movement, hormone levels, egg numbers and embryo scores are useful research measures, but they do not necessarily translate into pregnancy or live birth.

Look for randomized human trials of the actual ingredient, formulation and population. A 2026 review found no high-certainty evidence that the studied supplements improved female infertility outcomes compared with placebo. Some encouraging findings came from less reliable comparisons. Uncertainty is neither proof that every product works nor proof that every possible use is ineffective.

Supplements marketed for sperm health

Male fertility blends often combine antioxidants, zinc, selenium, folate, CoQ10 or carnitine. A better semen result alone does not establish that a couple is more likely to have a baby. AUA/ASRM guidance describes the clinical benefit of these supplements as uncertain; WHO’s 2025 guideline made no recommendation for or against antioxidants in infertile men with abnormal semen parameters.

In the 2025 SUMMER randomized trial, one antioxidant blend did not improve ongoing pregnancy compared with placebo alongside usual fertility care. This was not a test of every product, and ongoing pregnancy was not the same endpoint as live birth. A supplement should not replace semen assessment or treatment of an identified cause.

CoQ10 and ubiquinol: promising signals, limited certainty

Coenzyme Q10 participates in cellular energy production and has antioxidant activity. Ubiquinol is one form of CoQ10. Human fertility studies do exist: a 2024 review in women with diminished ovarian reserve undergoing IVF/ICSI reported improvements in some egg, embryo and clinical pregnancy outcomes, with important study-quality limitations.

These findings do not prove that CoQ10 reverses age-related changes, restores ovarian reserve or improves natural conception and live birth for everyone. A more expensive form is not automatically more effective. Discuss any proposed add-on with the fertility team; CoQ10 can interact with warfarin and insulin and may cause digestive upset or insomnia.

DHEA is a hormone, not an ordinary vitamin

Dehydroepiandrosterone, or DHEA, is a hormone precursor promoted for low ovarian reserve or poor response to IVF stimulation. Small or older positive studies should not be presented as an established treatment benefit. ESHRE’s 2025 ovarian-stimulation guideline recommends against DHEA before or during stimulation in both low and normal responders.

Do not start a retail DHEA product to improve egg quality or copy a study dose. Hormonal effects, your diagnosis, other medicines and the possibility of pregnancy require individual review. If a clinic proposes it, ask how that recommendation fits current guidance and what benefit, monitoring and stopping plan are expected.

Inositol and PCOS, now also called PMOS

Myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol are commonly marketed for polycystic ovary syndrome, renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) in 2026. The international guideline distinguishes possible metabolic effects from fertility treatment: inositol for infertility remains experimental because benefits and risks are too uncertain to recommend it as a fertility therapy.

Evidence for ovulation, clinical pregnancy and live birth is limited and inconsistent. No particular commercial ratio, dose or combination can be assumed best. Inositol does not replace assessment of irregular periods or evidence-based ovulation treatment when indicated; tell the clinician about products already being taken.

NAC, L-arginine and L-carnitine

N-acetylcysteine (NAC) has been studied particularly in women with ovulation problems. Changes in hormones or the thickness of the uterine lining are not proof of a higher live-birth rate. Recent reviews find signals worth researching, but insufficient certainty to make NAC a routine fertility treatment.

L-arginine and L-carnitine are different compounds with different biological roles. Arginine is linked to nitric-oxide pathways; carnitine helps cellular energy metabolism and is studied in sperm research. A concentration measured in follicular fluid, a plausible mechanism or improved sperm movement does not establish the benefit of taking a capsule. There is no universal fertility dose for self-treatment.

Antioxidants are not all interchangeable

Vitamin C, vitamin E, CoQ10, melatonin and green-tea compounds may appear under the same antioxidant label. That label does not make their effects, interactions or evidence equivalent. More antioxidant activity is not automatically better, and combining several products does not reproduce a clinical trial.

Melatonin is also a hormone; it can cause sleepiness and has insufficient pregnancy-safety research. Concentrated green-tea extracts differ from drinking tea and have occasionally been linked to liver injury. Neither should be added simply because a fertility advertisement calls it natural. Review the exact product with a pharmacist or clinician.

Vitex and other herbal hormone claims

Chasteberry, also called Vitex agnus-castus, is promoted for cycle symptoms and fertility. Evidence about premenstrual symptoms cannot be transferred to infertility. NCCIH finds insufficient reliable evidence that it helps infertility, and there are concerns about use in pregnancy and in hormone-sensitive conditions.

A herb that may influence hormonal pathways is not a harmless substitute for diagnosis. Vitex can cause stomach symptoms, headache or itching, and herbal products may interact with medicines. Do not assume that a regular-looking cycle after starting a product proves improved fertility or that it is safe to continue after conception.

Vitamins and minerals: meet needs without stacking

Folate and other B vitamins, vitamins C and E, zinc, magnesium and selenium are often included in fertility formulas. Zinc, magnesium and selenium are minerals, not vitamins. Treating an identified deficiency may be appropriate, but adding high doses when needs are met has not been established as a general fertility strategy.

Add up amounts across the prenatal, multivitamin, fertility blend and separate tablets. More is not necessarily safer. A clinician can advise whether diet, a health condition or a medicine creates a specific need. Avoid retinol-containing vitamin A supplements in pregnancy; use a suitable prenatal and obtain advice before adding extra nutrients.

What a label or quality seal can tell you

Check every ingredient, its amount per daily serving, serving size, manufacturer, batch and expiry date. A proprietary blend may hide individual quantities and make comparison difficult. Independent testing can help verify contents and contaminants, but a quality seal does not demonstrate fertility benefit or guarantee that a product is suitable for you.

Rules vary by country. In the United States, dietary supplements generally do not receive FDA approval before sale; manufacturers remain responsible for safety and truthful labeling, and FDA can inspect and take enforcement action. Sale in a pharmacy, a professional-looking website or a claim of good manufacturing practice does not mean a fertility treatment has been approved.

Check the research behind reviews and advertising

A pregnancy testimonial cannot establish what caused the pregnancy. Concurrent treatment, natural variation, selective reporting and paid promotion may explain a success story. Ask whether research studied the sold mixture or just one ingredient, whether participants resembled you, and whether the outcome was live birth rather than a laboratory measurement.

Look for a comparison group, study size, adverse effects, funding and whether independent researchers found similar results. Guarantees, pressure to buy and claims that one blend fixes every cause of infertility are warning signs. A spelling error alone is not proof of fraud, and an expensive price or a doctor’s photograph is not proof of benefit. Include repeat purchases in the cost decision.

Interactions and side effects need a real review

Bring photographs of all labels to the pharmacist or fertility team, including teas, powders, sports products and medicines. For example, St John’s wort can seriously interact with many medicines; CoQ10 can affect warfarin treatment; melatonin needs special review with blood thinners or epilepsy. A mixture can create risks that its marketing never mentions.

Side effects depend on the ingredient and dose and may include nausea, diarrhoea, headache, rash or sleep changes. Stop a suspected nonessential supplement and seek advice about a new reaction. Trouble breathing, facial or tongue swelling or collapse needs emergency care. Yellowing of the eyes or skin, dark urine or severe abdominal pain warrants urgent medical assessment.

Do not postpone fertility assessment

For regular unprotected intercourse without pregnancy, assessment is generally advised after 12 months when the person providing eggs is under 35, or after 6 months at 35 or older. Over 40, seek advice sooner. Irregular or absent periods, suspected endometriosis, known sperm problems or other relevant conditions justify earlier assessment.

Both partners should be assessed when applicable. An online fertility blend cannot detect blocked tubes, explain absent ovulation or replace evaluation of sperm production. Do not spend successive months trying different bottles while delaying care. If an add-on is considered, agree on its purpose, evidence, cost, review date and place alongside the treatment plan.

Plan for a positive pregnancy test

Review nonessential fertility products before conception rather than waiting for a positive test. Some have little pregnancy-safety information; others contain hormones, herbs or unsuitable nutrient amounts. Ask in advance which products to stop, which to continue and whom to contact if pregnancy occurs.

A positive test is not a reason to abruptly stop all medicines or appropriate folic acid and prenatal care. Contact the prescriber or pharmacist promptly to review the exact list. Continue prescribed treatment as directed while obtaining advice; do not substitute a fertility blend for a pregnancy-appropriate supplement.

A practical decision before buying

Write down the problem you hope to address and ask: is there a deficiency or diagnosis, what outcome might improve, and how certain is that evidence for someone like me? Then check the actual formulation, interactions, pregnancy plan and total cost. Choosing not to buy an unproven add-on is a reasonable decision.

No supplement can promise conception, erase age-related fertility changes or replace necessary treatment. A balanced diet, appropriate folic acid, relevant medical care and timely assessment provide a stronger foundation than a long supplement list. Decisions can be shared with a clinician without treating uncertainty as a sales opportunity.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Distinguish routine preconception nutrition from fertility treatment claims and trial outcomes.

Use current fertility guidelines, primary trial reports and systematic reviews to describe uncertainty accurately.

Review labels, interactions and pregnancy safety with a qualified clinician or pharmacist.

How BeMama can help

BeMama presents the full fertility-supplement decision without endorsing a brand or promising conception.

When to seek help

This information supports a discussion with your care team and does not prescribe a supplement regimen. Seek timely fertility assessment and urgent help for severe reactions.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Folic acid before pregnancy prevents neural tube defects; fertility blends make a different claim.
  • Egg, sperm or hormone changes do not automatically mean more live births.
  • DHEA, inositol, antioxidants and herbs have different evidence and safety limits.
  • Check all ingredient amounts, interactions and the pregnancy plan before buying.
  • Do not delay fertility assessment while trying successive products.

Frequently asked questions

Can fertility supplements interact with medicines?

Yes. The risk depends on the full ingredient list and medicines. Bring labels to a pharmacist or fertility clinician; natural products and combinations can cause important interactions.

Do they have side effects?

They can cause digestive symptoms, headache, rash, sleep changes or more serious ingredient-specific problems. Dose, combinations, existing illness and pregnancy matter; a quality seal does not remove these risks.

How are they supposed to work?

Claims often involve nutrient replacement, energy metabolism, antioxidant activity or hormone pathways. A plausible mechanism is not proof that taking the product improves pregnancy or live birth.

Can they replace fertility treatment?

No. They cannot substitute for identifying a cause or for indicated treatment. Correcting a deficiency may be part of care, while optional add-ons require separate evidence and a review plan.

Is there one best fertility multivitamin?

No formula has been established as best for everyone. Nutritional needs, medicines and the cause of fertility difficulty differ. A suitable prenatal is not the same as a proven infertility treatment.

Does CoQ10 improve egg quality after 40?

Some IVF studies report encouraging intermediate outcomes, but this does not prove reversal of age-related changes or a higher live-birth rate for everyone. Do not delay age-appropriate fertility advice.

Should I take DHEA or inositol without a prescription?

Availability does not establish suitability. Current ESHRE guidance recommends against DHEA for ovarian-stimulation add-on use in low and normal responders; inositol for PMOS-related infertility remains experimental.

What if I become pregnant while taking a blend?

Contact a clinician or pharmacist promptly with the exact label. Review nonessential add-ons, but do not abruptly stop prescribed medicines or appropriate folic acid and prenatal care without advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
